name: Lycopene

lead: Lycopene is the red pigment in cooked tomatoes, watermelon and pink grapefruit, and people take it for healthier-looking, slightly warmer skin and as an internal helper against UV damage.

It is fat-soluble and collects in skin, where it quenches reactive oxygen species generated by UV light. That can blunt part of the sunburn response. A 2024 systematic review of 21 intervention trials associated tomato and lycopene intake with less UV-related redness and a higher minimal erythema dose, plus changes in skin thickness and density. The European Food Safety Authority concluded there was insufficient evidence for antioxidant effects in humans.

paras: It is taken through cooked tomato products eaten with fat, which improves absorption, or through supplements. Skin effects in trials appeared over weeks to months of daily intake. People use it alongside sunscreen, not in place of it.

Dietary and supplement amounts are generally well tolerated. Very high intake can cause lycopenemia, a harmless orange tint that fades after intake is reduced. Possible interactions with blood-pressure drugs and anticoagulants have been noted. Many trials are small and use tomato paste or industry-supplied extracts.

angle.text: Lycopene from cooked tomatoes or supplements settles into the skin as an antioxidant, aiming to cut UV-related redness and damage and give a warmer tint over time. Trials have measured reduced UV-induced redness and changes in skin thickness and density.

lead: Lycopene is a bright red carotenoid hydrocarbon found in tomatoes, watermelon, pink grapefruit, red guava and some other red fruits and vegetables. Unlike beta-carotene, it has no vitamin A activity, and it is also used as a food colour (E160d) [1][2]. It is taken through food, especially cooked tomato products eaten with fat, and as a supplement [1][2].

In skincare and appearance contexts, lycopene is promoted as an internal antioxidant that may reduce UV-related skin damage and give a warmer tone. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 intervention trials found that tomato and lycopene supplementation was associated with reductions in erythema-related measures, MMP-1, ICAM-1 and skin pigmentation, and increases in minimal erythema dose, skin thickness and density [3]. Regulators have taken a more cautious view: the European Food Safety Authority concluded there was insufficient evidence for antioxidant effects in humans, including in skin [1].

High intake can cause lycopenemia, an orange skin discolouration that is expected to fade after intake is reduced [1]. Lycopene is non-toxic in dietary amounts, though intolerance, interactions with blood-pressure drugs and anticoagulants have been noted [1].

paras: Lycopene is taken as a tomato-derived supplement or through cooked tomato products in the hope of photoprotection and a warmer complexion [3][4]. Topical formulations such as a lycopene emulgel have also been tested for skin biophysical parameters [5].

It is not an essential nutrient, and the median and 99th percentile of dietary intake have been estimated at 5.2 and 123 mg per day [1]. It is marketed in prostate and cardiovascular supplements on the basis of antioxidant activity [6][7].

Skin: the 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 intervention trials in healthy subjects reported that tomato and lycopene supplementation was associated with significant reductions in delta-a* (redness), MMP-1, ICAM-1 and skin pigmentation, and increases in minimal erythema dose, skin thickness and skin density; the authors concluded it could reduce erythema and improve skin appearance [3]. A 2002 review discussed carotenoids and protection against solar UV radiation [4]. A topical lycopene emulgel trial reported improved biophysical skin parameters [5], and a registered study evaluated a tomato-extract product on skin attributes in 50 healthy participants [8].

Cardiovascular and other outcomes: reviews describe an inconsistent evidence base. A 2020 review of randomized trials found conflicting evidence on cardiovascular risk factors, while a 2017 review concluded that tomato products and lycopene reduced blood lipids and blood pressure [1]. Review articles note epidemiological associations with lower cardiovascular risk with some controversy [6][7]. A registered trial tested different doses on blood pressure in pre-hypertensive adults and was terminated [9]. For prostate cancer, a 2015 review found dietary lycopene associated with reduced risk while a 2021 meta-analysis found no effect [1]; registered trials include metastatic prostate cancer [10].

Bioavailability studies show absorption is enhanced by fat and cooking and has been studied with added black pepper and oil [1][11][12]. A registered study examined lycopene and sperm quality [13]. Many skin trials are small and some use industry-supplied extracts.

Lycopene is non-toxic and commonly eaten. Reported problems include intolerance or allergic reaction with diarrhoea, nausea, stomach pain and loss of appetite, a possible increased bleeding risk with anticoagulants, and possible interactions with blood-pressure drugs. Lycopenemia, an orange skin discolouration, occurs with high intakes [1].

Lycopene is a highly lipophilic antioxidant with eleven conjugated double bonds, and absorption requires bile salts and fat micelles; absorption is enhanced by fat and by cooking, and oil-based supplements may be absorbed more efficiently than food [1][2]. In human blood, cis-isomers make up more than 60 percent of total lycopene [1].

It is a symmetrical tetraterpene derived from eight isoprene units, with all-trans form predominating in plants. Isolation procedures were first reported in 1910 and the structure was determined by 1931 [1]. It is an intermediate in biosynthesis of beta-carotene and other carotenoids [1].

EFSA concluded there was insufficient evidence for antioxidant effects of lycopene in humans, including in skin and for protecting vision from UV light. In 2005 the US FDA rejected requests to allow qualified labelling for lycopene and reduced cancer risks, concluding there was no credible evidence supporting such a relationship [1].

The sampled community material is mostly on T Nation and focuses on prostate and urinary health rather than skin tone: forum members discuss lycopene as part of prostate-support supplement blends and mention it for blood pressure and urinary symptoms [14][15][16][17]. Some members mention that ketchup contains lycopene [18].

lore.intro: On T Nation, lycopene appears mainly as a prostate-support or heart-health ingredient in supplement stacks [14][15][16].
